title: Adaptive prefetch controller for heterogeneous prompt/response flows
creator: Lina Chen
description:
Problem:
Mixed prompt/response workloads (short prompts + long temperature-generated responses and vice-versa) are causing suboptimal continuous-batcher behavior: excessive KV-cache thrash, GPU memory fragmentation, and intermittent p99 latency spikes during microbursts. Our existing length-agnostic prefetch window and uniform slot tenure allow small dialogues to displace long-running KV residency, which increases cold-KV rehydration and slows tails for latency-sensitive customers.

Goal:
Design and ship an adaptive prefetch controller that reduces KV eviction churn for heterogeneous dialogue flows, minimizes GPU memory fragmentation, and preserves latency SLOs while maintaining throughput. The controller should operate inside the continuous batching scheduler and be togglable behind a feature flag for canary rollouts.

Proposed approach (high level):
1) Prefetch window adaptation: maintain a compact per-customer/dialogue length distribution sketch and use it to compute a dynamic prefetch window size. Short-dialogue-heavy tenants get narrower prefetch windows; long-dialogue-heavy tenants get wider windows with soft pinning of long KV pages.
2) Residency scoring: compute per-slot residency score that factors: recent token density, expected remaining tokens (length estimator), and last-access recency. Prefer retaining high-score slots on eviction.
3) Soft pinning and hysteresis: allow temporary pinning of long-response slots with a decaying TTL and hysteresis thresholds to avoid ping-pong evictions when workloads shift.
4) Fragmentation-aware packing: when allocating GPU slabs, prefer consolidating contiguous slot allocations (slab-aware packing) to increase contiguous free memory run lengths and reduce fragmentation.
5) Backpressure integration: integrate prefetch controller signals into admission control so that when KV eviction pressure rises, admission policy will more aggressively favor shorter sequences or fallback model variants.
6) Metrics, canary & fallback: expose metrics and a feature-flagged canary path with automatic fallback to baseline policy if p99 latency or KV eviction rate regresses.

Experiments and validation plan:
- Synthetic workloads: create mixed-turn traces with controlled short/long ratios (10/90, 50/50, 90/10) and microburst patterns to exercise corner cases.
- Scale tests: run canary on 1% of traffic on a Dedicated pool with 8x A100s and compare baseline vs adaptive controller.
- A/B metrics: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, KV eviction rate, contiguous free slab size, GPU utilization variance, cost-per-token.
- Regression criteria: p99 latency regression < 5% vs baseline, KV eviction rate decreased by >= 20% on long-response heavy traces, throughput within +/-3% of baseline for mixed workloads, contiguous free slab size increased by >= 15%.

Implementation milestones:
- Design doc (this ticket) + measurement harness: 1 week.
- Core controller prototype (scheduler hook + lightweight sketch): 2 weeks.
- Packing allocator adjustments (slab-aware hints): 1 week.
- Canary rollout + observability (dashboards + alerts): 1 week.
- Iteration and full rollout: 1 week.

Acceptance criteria:
- Controller deployed behind feature flag and exercised on synthetic traces with measurable improvements per regression criteria.
- End-to-end canary run shows stable p99 tail for 72h on mixed production-like traffic.
- Playbook for rollback and incident runbook documented in Confluence.
- Unit tests cover residency scoring and pin/unpin lifecycle; integration tests for slab packing.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Over-pinning could reduce effective throughput. Mitigation: soft TTL + global admission backpressure and canary checks.
- Risk: Incorrect length estimation under adversarial prompts. Mitigation: conservative estimator fallback and fast decay of pinning weight on mismatches.
